passage: Note to the file, Class 4, Thursday. Tarun, nine, came to me and asked, "Ma'am, why does Mala always sit at the end of the bench alone?" He also said, "Vinod's mother told him Mala's mother cleans their house, so Mala isn't like us." I did not brush the question aside. I told Tarun that some people treat others as lesser because of the work their family does or the surname they carry, that it is unfair, and that Mala is the same as everyone in the class. He thought, then said, "Then I'll sit by her." The next day I saw him carrying his lunch box to the end of the bench. I have spoken to Vinod and will talk with the class about kindness. Kalyani

qa.q: Where does Mala always sit?
qa.a: Mala always sits at the end of the bench alone.

qa.q: What does Tarun's "Then I'll sit by her" suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: Tarun feels concern and a wish to be fair. Once the teacher explained, he was ready to act at once.

qa.q: Which choice by the teacher mattered when Tarun asked his question?
qa.a: The teacher did not brush the question aside. The teacher explained that treating people as lesser is unfair and that Mala is the same as everyone in the class.

qa.q: How might Mala feel when Tarun carries his lunch box to the end of the bench?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone, since a classmate chose to sit beside Mala without being asked.

grounding: A child notices who sits apart and whose parents work in a house, and an adult's calm explanation leads the child toward fairness.

passage: Saturday. Today Pooja came with her Aai, who cleans our house on Saturdays. Pooja waited on the outside step and did not come in, even though it was hot. I asked Mummy why. Mummy said, "That is how it is. Don't ask silly questions." I gave Pooja water in my own steel glass, and she looked at it for a long time before drinking. Later I saw Mummy wash the glass twice. At school Pooja is the fastest at maths, but at lunch she sits alone because some girls say her surname is "different". Papa said tonight that everyone in a house should be treated well, and I said I know. I'm going to ask Pooja to sit with me on Monday. Kunal

qa.q: Where did Pooja wait while her Aai worked?
qa.a: Pooja waited on the outside step and did not come in, even though it was hot.

qa.q: What is Kunal feeling about how Pooja was treated?
qa.a: Kunal feels uneasy and sad about it. Kunal asks Mummy why, hands Pooja water, and decides to ask Pooja to sit together.

qa.q: What choice did Kunal make after the Saturday visit?
qa.a: Kunal decided to ask Pooja to sit together on Monday, so at lunch she is not left alone.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt looking at the steel glass for a long time?
qa.a: Possibly unsure and careful, since she was being offered something she was not used to being offered, and glad to be treated kindly.

grounding: A child notices which children wait outside, whose parents work in the house and whose surname is teased, and hears different adult explanations.

passage:
At the village school in Barmer, the midday meal came in big steel buckets. Irfan, nine, noticed that three children always sat by the far wall, away from the rest.
"Why do they sit there?" he asked his friend.
"My dadi says their family is different. We shouldn't sit with them."
Irfan didn't understand, but he stayed in his place.
The next day, Bidisha Madam noticed where Irfan was looking. At lunch, she carried her own plate to the far wall and sat down there. "Everyone eats together in my school," she said. "Nobody is less than anybody."
Irfan picked up his plate and went to sit beside her. One by one, others followed.

qa.q: Where did the three children always sit?
qa.a: They always sat by the far wall, away from the rest.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when he stayed in his place?
qa.a: He felt confused and unsure, because he didn't understand why his friend's dadi said the family was different.

qa.q: How did Bidisha Madam handle it well?
qa.a: She showed fairness through action, sitting with the separated children herself, and explained clearly that nobody is less than anybody.

qa.q: How might the children by the wall feel when the others joined them?
qa.a: They might feel included and relieved, no longer marked out as different at every meal.

grounding: A child notices which children sit apart and hears an adult's prejudice, and a teacher's example shapes fairness instead.

passage:
In Kwame's class in Leeds, a boy kept calling Paulo "Paul-NO" and laughing. Kwame, ten, didn't join in, but he didn't stop it either.
Then on Saturday, Kwame went to play at a classmate's big house and saw Paulo's mum there, mopping the kitchen floor. Paulo's mum smiled at him. The classmate's dad said, "Don't bother the cleaner."
At dinner, Kwame asked, "Is Paulo poorer than us? Is that why they tease him?"
His mother put her fork down. "Paulo's mum works hard, like I do at the hospital. Some people have more money. It doesn't make them better. And names aren't for mocking."
On Monday, when the boy said "Paul-NO," Kwame said, "His name's Paulo," and sat next to him.

qa.q: What did the boy keep calling Paulo?
qa.a: The boy kept calling Paulo "Paul-NO" and laughing.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling when he asked about Paulo at dinner?
qa.a: He was curious and troubled, trying to understand whether being poorer was why Paulo got teased.

qa.q: What did Kwame's mother do that shaped his view?
qa.a: She explained calmly that working hard is honourable, that having more money doesn't make people better, and that names aren't for mocking.

qa.q: How might Paulo feel when Kwame sits next to him?
qa.a: Paulo would likely feel supported and less alone after being teased about his name.

grounding: A child notices whose parent works in another's home and whose name gets teased, and an adult's explanation shapes fairness.

passage:
In Class 6 at the city school, the teacher took attendance by full name. Every time she said Harsha's surname, two boys at the back snorted.
Himani, eleven, noticed. She noticed that Harsha now said "present" before his name was finished. She noticed he ate lunch in the library.
She told her father that evening. "Why do they laugh at his surname? It's just a name."
Her father was quiet. "Some people think certain surnames mean a lower family. It's an old, wrong idea, and it hurts people."
"Should I tell Miss?"
"Yes. And you can sit with him."
The next day, Himani told the class teacher at break. At lunch she found Harsha in the library and opened her tiffin beside him.

qa.q: Where did Harsha eat lunch?
qa.a: Harsha ate lunch in the library.

qa.q: How can you tell Himani felt troubled by what she noticed?
qa.a: She kept noticing small signs, like Harsha rushing to say "present" and eating in the library, and raised it with her father that evening.

qa.q: What did Himani's father say that helped her act fairly?
qa.a: He named the laughter as an old, wrong idea that hurts people, and encouraged her to tell the teacher and sit with Harsha.

qa.q: What is it like for Harsha when his surname is read aloud?
qa.a: He seems ashamed and anxious, trying to say "present" before his name is finished so fewer people hear it.

grounding: A child notices a classmate's surname being mocked, and a parent's explanation leads her toward fairness.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: I'm Aparna, and I sit near the window in Class 4. I notice things. Francis always eats his lunch on the steps, not at our table. His mother cooks at our house in the mornings, and at school some boys call him "Francis-cook". He never answers. He just eats faster. One evening I asked Papa why Francis's mother makes our rotis but never sits on our sofa. Papa put his newspaper down. "She can sit wherever she likes. Aunty works for us; she is not less than us." The next morning he asked her to sit and have tea with him. I don't know what Francis feels about any of it. Today I carried my tiffin to the steps and sat down beside him.

qa.q: Where does Francis eat his lunch?
qa.a: Francis eats his lunch on the steps, not at the table.

qa.q: What might Aparna be feeling when asking Papa about the sofa?
qa.a: Aparna seems curious and a little uneasy, noticing something that feels unfair and wanting it explained.

qa.q: What did Papa's reply and action teach that a lecture could not?
qa.a: By saying she is not less and then inviting her to sit for tea, Papa showed fairness in action, and Aparna copied it the next day at school.

qa.q: What might it be like for Francis when some boys call him "Francis-cook"?
qa.a: It likely hurts and embarrasses him; he stays silent and eats faster, as if trying to get away from the teasing.

grounding: It illustrates a child noticing who sits apart, whose parent works in the house and whose name is teased, and how a parent's fair explanation shapes the child's own conduct.
